facts.statement: The species Limusaurus inextricabilis was described in 2009 from fossils found in the Upper Shishugou Formation in the Junggar Basin of China.
facts.quote: The type and only species Limusaurus inextricabilis was described in 2009 from specimens found in the Upper Shishugou Formation in the Junggar Basin of China.

facts.statement: Limusaurus underwent a drastic transformation as it aged, losing its juvenile teeth and developing a beak as an adult.
facts.quote: It underwent a drastic morphological transformation as it aged: while juveniles were toothed, these teeth were completely lost and replaced by a beak with age.

facts.statement: The loss of teeth in adult Limusaurus likely indicated a dietary shift from omnivory to herbivory, supported by the presence of gastroliths in adults.
facts.quote: The change to toothlessness in adults probably corresponded to a dietary shift from omnivory to herbivory, which is confirmed by the presence of gastroliths (stomach stones) in adults.

facts.statement: Limusaurus shares convergent features with later ornithomimid theropods and earlier non-dinosaurian shuvosaurids.
facts.quote: Several of these features were convergently similar to the later ornithomimid theropods as well as the earlier non-dinosaurian shuvosaurids.

facts.statement: Limusaurus was the first known ceratosaur from Asia and belongs to the family Noasauridae, closely related to Elaphrosaurus.
facts.quote: Limusaurus was the first known member of the group Ceratosauria from Asia. It belonged to the Noasauridae, a family of small and lightly built ceratosaurs, along with its closest relative Elaphrosaurus.

facts.statement: Paleontologist Xu Xing and colleagues described and named Limusaurus inextricabilis in 2009.
facts.quote: In 2009, the small ceratosaur was described by paleontologist Xu Xing and colleagues, who named it Limusaurus inextricabilis.

facts.statement: The name Limusaurus inextricabilis means "mud lizard impossible to extricate," referring to the hypothesis that the specimens died after being stuck in mud.
facts.quote: The genus name consists of the words limus, Latin for "mud" or "mire", and saurus, Greek for "lizard", and the species name means "impossible to extricate"; both names refer to how these specimens appear to have died after being mired.

facts.statement: Seventeen additional specimens of Limusaurus were described in 2017 by Shuo Wang and colleagues from the same fossil blocks as the original 2009 discovery.
facts.quote: Seventeen additional Limusaurus specimens were described by paleontologist Shuo Wang and colleagues in 2017, excavated from the same blocks as those described in 2009.

facts.statement: Toothless adults and toothed juveniles of Limusaurus were initially thought to be different species but were later identified as the same species.
facts.quote: The toothless adults and toothed juveniles were initially thought to be different kinds of dinosaurs, and were studied separately, until it was realized they represent the same species.

facts.statement: One adult specimen of Limusaurus is estimated to be 15% larger than the holotype.
facts.quote: One adult specimen is estimated to have been 15% larger than the holotype.

facts.statement: Although Limusaurus may have had feathers, there is no direct fossil evidence confirming this.
facts.quote: While Limusaurus has sometimes been depicted with feathers and may have had them, there is no direct evidence of such structures.

facts.statement: The pattern of digit reduction in Limusaurus supports a contested hypothesis regarding the evolution of the three-fingered hand in tetanuran theropods and birds.
facts.quote: The pattern of digit reduction in Limusaurus has been used to support the hypothesis that the three-fingered hand of tetanuran theropods is the result of the loss of the first and fifth digits from the ancestral five-fingered theropod hand, a contested hypothesis which is relevant to the evolution of birds.

facts.statement: Limusaurus possessed an elongated neck with long cervical vertebrae similar to those of Elaphrosaurus.
facts.quote: The cervicals (neck vertebrae) of Limusaurus were elongated as in the closely related Elaphrosaurus, and the neck itself was long.

facts.statement: The shoulder blade of Limusaurus featured a distinctive prominent ridge along its front edge.
facts.quote: Distinctively, the scapula (shoulder blade) bore a prominent ridge at its front edge.

facts.statement: Limusaurus had a sternum fused into a single large continuous plate, a trait that evolved independently in coelurosaurs.
facts.quote: The sternum was fused into a single, large, continuous plate, another feature that evolved independently in coelurosaurs (convergent evolution).

facts.statement: Limusaurus possessed a furcula, or wishbone, which was previously unknown among ceratosaurians.
facts.quote: Limusaurus also had a furcula, or wishbone, which previously was unknown among ceratosaurians.

facts.statement: Limusaurus had only three fingers, uniquely missing the first finger entirely, with the first metacarpal shorter than the others.
facts.quote: Limusaurus had three fingers (the middle three), as compared to the five fingers of more basal relatives; it was unique in that the first finger was missing entirely, and the first metacarpal was shorter than the other metacarpals.

facts.statement: The second metacarpal of Limusaurus was more robust than the other metacarpals, a distinctive feature of the genus.
facts.quote: The second metacarpal was more robust than the other metacarpals, which is another distinctive feature of the genus.

facts.statement: Limusaurus had three phalanges on both the second and third fingers, whereas other early theropods typically had four on the third finger.
facts.quote: The second finger had three phalanges (finger bones). The third finger also only had three phalanges, as opposed to four in other early theropods.

facts.statement: Limusaurus had legs adapted for running, with the tibiotarsus 1.2 times and the foot 1.3 times the length of the femur.
facts.quote: The elongated legs of Limusaurus had proportions that were well-adapted to running, with their lower segments much longer than the femur: the tibiotarsus, the fusion of the tibia (shin bone) and tarsal bones, was 1.2 times the length of the femur, and the foot was 1.3 times the length of the femur.

facts.statement: The legs of Limusaurus were 1.8 times the length of its torso.
facts.quote: The legs were 1.8 times the length of the torso.

facts.statement: The finger claw bones of Limusaurus were short, stout, expanded at the base, and featured two grooves on their sides.
facts.quote: The unguals (claw bones) of the fingers were short, stout, and expanded at their base. They had two grooves on their sides, a feature also found in Masiakasaurus.

facts.statement: Xu and colleagues classified Limusaurus as a basal member of Ceratosauria in 2009.
facts.quote: Limusaurus was classified as a basal member of Ceratosauria by Xu and colleagues in 2009 (who also considered the closely related Elaphrosaurus as such).

facts.statement: A 2016 study by Rauhut and Carrano placed Limusaurus within the abelisauroid family Noasauridae.
facts.quote: A 2016 study by paleontologists Oliver Rauhut and Matthew Carrano found Limusaurus to be more derived, grouping together with Elaphrosaurus within the abelisauroid family Noasauridae.

facts.statement: Baiano and colleagues found in 2020 that Limusaurus formed a clade with Elaphrosaurus and the genus Huinculsaurus.
facts.quote: Argentinian paleontologist Mattia Baiano and colleagues, in 2020, found Limusaurus to form a clade with Elaphrosaurus as well as with the new genus Huinculsaurus.

facts.statement: Limusaurus lived during the Oxfordian stage of the Jurassic period, approximately 161 to 157 million years ago.
facts.quote: In addition to being the first definite ceratosaur known from Asia to be discovered, Limusaurus is also one of the earliest known members of the group, living during the Oxfordian stage of the Jurassic period (approximately 161-157 million years ago).

facts.statement: Limusaurus is considered the earliest known toothless theropod and the only non-bird theropod with strong bilateral reduction of its digits.
facts.quote: Biologist Josef Stiegler and colleagues stated in a 2014 conference abstract that Limusaurus is the earliest known toothless theropod, as well as the only non-bird theropod known to have had strong bilateral reduction of its digits (as the outer fingers were reduced in size).

facts.statement: Studies indicate that Limusaurus underwent extreme anatomical changes during growth, with juvenile specimens grouping separately from adults.
facts.quote: To test the influence of the extreme anatomical changes with growth in Limusaurus, Wang and colleagues, in their 2017 study, performed separate analyses that were based on only the adult anatomy or on both the adult and juvenile anatomy.

facts.statement: Researchers initially used Limusaurus to support the Bilateral Digit Reduction hypothesis regarding the evolution of bird hands.
facts.quote: Limusaurus was initially considered as evidence for the BDR hypothesis by Xu and colleagues in 2009 due to it—and other ceratosaurians—having a reduced first digit

facts.statement: A 2016 analysis suggests the reduced digits in Limusaurus were caused by a specific developmental anomaly unique to ceratosaurians rather than a shared evolutionary trait with birds.
facts.quote: As demonstrated by a teratological analysis by biologist Geoffrey Guinard in 2016, the abbreviation (mesomelia) and loss of digits (hypophalangia) in the forelimb of Limusaurus is likely the result of a developmental anomaly that appeared exclusively in and persisted throughout the evolutionary lineage of ceratosaurians

facts.statement: Fossil specimens of Limusaurus exhibit 78 distinct anatomical changes associated with growth.
facts.quote: Specimens of Limusaurus show 78 different anatomical changes that occurred as the animals grew

facts.statement: Limusaurus is notable for completely losing its teeth as it matured from juvenile to adult stages.

facts.statement: Limusaurus ranks among the very few known jawed vertebrates to completely lose its teeth during its lifetime.
facts.quote: Limusaurus is one of the few known jawed vertebrates where teeth are completely lost during growth

facts.statement: The fibrolamellar bone structure of Limusaurus indicates that the animal grew rapidly.
facts.quote: The bone tissue was primarily composed of fibrolamellar bone (where the internal fibres are disorganized), indicating that Limusaurus grew quickly

facts.statement: All teeth were missing in Limusaurus specimens that were older than one year.

facts.statement: Adult Limusaurus specimens contained gastroliths, which were larger and more numerous in older adults than in younger ones.

facts.statement: Isotope analysis confirmed that adult Limusaurus had diets matching those of other herbivorous dinosaurs.
facts.quote: An isotope analysis of the available specimens of Limusaurus likewise showed that adults consistently match the isotope signatures of other herbivorous dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Isotopic evidence suggests juvenile Limusaurus were likely omnivorous before switching to a strict herbivorous diet as adults.
facts.quote: In the same analysis, juveniles and subadults were found to vary greatly in their isotopic signatures; this indicates that juveniles were likely omnivorous (feeding on both animals and plants), but switched to strict herbivory as they aged.

facts.statement: Paleontologists suggested that Limusaurus likely lived in groups based on the abundance of fossils and evidence of rapid burial.
facts.quote: These authors also suggested that the abundance of Limusaurus inferred for the area and the evidence for successive, rapid burials of each individual made it possible that Limusaurus was gregarious, living in groups.

facts.statement: In 2018, paleontologist Rafael Delcourt agreed that the multiple-specimen assemblages of Limusaurus suggest these small ceratosaurs lived in groups.
facts.quote: Paleontologist Rafael Delcourt agreed in 2018 that since both Limusaurus and Masiakasaurus have been found in assemblages of multiple specimens each, this suggests these small ceratosaurs lived in groups.

facts.statement: Limusaurus lived during the Late Jurassic, approximately 161 to 157 million years ago.
facts.quote: The formation is dated to the Late Jurassic, around 161 to 157 million years ago.

facts.statement: Limusaurus fossils are found in environments ranging from alluvial fans and plains to streams, wetlands, and shallow lakes.
facts.quote: Limusaurus occurs in the upper part of the formation, which represents a variety of environments, including alluvial fans and alluvial plains, streams, wetlands, and shallow lakes.

facts.statement: The climate where Limusaurus lived was likely highly seasonal with warm, wet summers and dry winters due to monsoonal influences.
facts.quote: The climate was probably highly seasonal due to monsoonal influences, with warm, wet summers and dry winters.

facts.statement: The environment supported a rich forest dominated by Araucaria trees, with undergrowth consisting of ferns, horsetails, and shrubs.
facts.quote: The climate enabled the growth of a richly forested environment; the forest would have been dominated by Araucaria trees, with the undergrowth being occupied by Coniopteris, Anglopteris and Osmunda ferns, Equisetites horsetails, and Elatocladus shrubs.

facts.statement: The ecosystem where Limusaurus lived contained more than 35 vertebrate species, including at least 14 dinosaur species.
facts.quote: More than 35 species of vertebrates are known from fossils, including at least 14 dinosaur species.

facts.statement: Large numbers of Limusaurus fossils in the mud pits likely result from the tendency of small animals to get trapped in mud.
facts.quote: The size of these assemblages can be attributed to the tendency of smaller animals to become trapped in mud.

facts.statement: Evidence suggests one Limusaurus carcass was pushed to the bottom of a pit by the trampling of another animal trapped later.

facts.statement: Limusaurus specimens typically show flexed hind limbs, indicating they died in a resting pose within the mud pits.

facts.statement: The jaw fenestra was quite large, accounting for 40% of the total length of the lower jaw.

facts.statement: The arms and hands of Limusaurus were considerably reduced, even more so than in Ceratosaurus.
facts.quote: Los brazos y las manos de Limusaurus se redujeron considerablemente, incluso más que el de Ceratosaurus.

facts.statement: The first finger was smaller than the others and completely lacked phalanges.

facts.statement: The sternum fused into a single, large, continuous plate, representing an evolutionary convergence with coelurosaurs.

facts.statement: It possesses a furcula or wishbone, which was previously unknown among ceratosaurians.

facts.statement: The first toe of each foot, or hallux, was extremely reduced, being only 17% of the length of the third metatarsal.

facts.statement: The presence of gastroliths in both specimens and a toothless beak suggest a herbivorous diet, making it the most basal theropod to show this type of diet.

facts.statement: Limusaurus is a very basal ceratosaurian that retains four fingers in the hand (digits I–II-III-IV), with digit I strongly reduced.

facts.statement: It is the first defined ceratosaurian discovered from East Asia and one of the earliest.
facts.quote: Es el primer ceratosauriano definido del este de Asia que se descubriera y de uno de los más tempranos.

facts.statement: Its discovery demonstrates that Asian dinosaur fauna was less endemic during the Middle to Late Jurassic than thought and suggests a possible land connection between Asia and other continents during that period.
facts.quote: Su descubrimiento demuestra que la fauna dinosauriana asiática era menos endémica durante el Jurásico medio a tardío de lo que se pensó y sugiere una posible conexión terrestre entre Asia y otros continentes durante ese período.

facts.statement: Histological analysis of growth lines in Limusaurus tibiae indicates the animal reached skeletal maturity at 6 years of age.
facts.quote: El análisis histológico de las líneas de crecimiento detenido dentro de las tibias de las diversas etapas ontogenéticas de Limusaurus indica que el animal estaba esqueléticamente maduro a los 6 años de edad.

facts.statement: Specimens of Limusaurus show 78 distinct anatomical changes that occurred as the animals grew.
facts.quote: Los especímenes de Limusaurus muestran 78 cambios anatómicos diferentes que ocurrieron a medida que los animales crecieron.

facts.statement: The most obvious change during Limusaurus growth is the complete loss of teeth from juveniles to adults.
facts.quote: El cambio más obvio que ocurrió durante el crecimiento de Limusaurus es la pérdida completa de dientes de juveniles a adultos.

facts.statement: Juvenile Limusaurus began with a total of 42 teeth: one in the premaxilla, eight in the maxilla, and eleven in the lower jaw.
facts.quote: Los juveniles comenzaron con un diente en la premaxila, ocho en el maxilar y once en la mandíbula inferior, 42 dientes en total.

facts.statement: All teeth are missing in subadult and adult Limusaurus specimens older than one year of age.
facts.quote: En especímenes subadultos y adultos mayores de un año de edad, faltan todos los dientes.

facts.statement: The loss of teeth with age in Limusaurus represents the most extreme case of age-related dental morphology change among dinosaurs.
facts.quote: La pérdida de dientes con la edad en Limusaurus es el caso más extremo de morfología dental que cambia con la edad entre los dinosaurios.

facts.statement: Limusaurus is one of the few known vertebrates with jaws where teeth are lost completely during ontogeny, alongside species like bearded rockfish, rockfish, several gars, and the platypus.
facts.quote: La pérdida de dientes con la edad en Limusaurus es el caso más extremo de morfología dental que cambia con la edad entre los dinosaurios. De hecho, Limusaurus es uno de los pocos vertebrados con mandíbula conocidos donde los dientes se pierden por completo durante la ontogenia, los otros son el salmonete barbado y el Salmonete de roca, varios coridoras y el ornitorrinco.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the temporary interruption in tooth replacement in Limusaurus is likely due to the regression of tooth buds, similar to the veiled chameleon.
facts.quote: La interrupción temporal en el reemplazo de dientes probablemente se deba a la regresión de las yemas de los dientes, como en el camaleón velado.

facts.statement: Adult Limusaurus specimens show herbivory-associated morphological traits shared with other herbivorous theropod groups like Ornithomimosauria, Therizinosauria, Oviraptorosauria, Alvarezsauroidea, and the troodontid Jinfengopteryx.
facts.quote: Los especímenes adultos de Limusaurus muestran rasgos morfológicos asociados con la herbivoría que se comparten con otros grupos de terópodos herbívoros, como Ornithomimosauria, Therizinosauria , Oviraptorosauria y Alvarezsauroidea, junto con el trodóntido Jinfengopteryx.

facts.statement: Adult Limusaurus samples are characterized by the presence of gastroliths, with older adults having larger and more numerous gastroliths than younger adults.
facts.quote: En particular, las muestras de adultos se caracterizan por la presencia de cálculos estomacales, gastrolitos, con adultos mayores que tienen gastrolitos más grandes y numerosos que los adultos más jóvenes.

facts.statement: The increase in gastrolith quantity in older adults may indicate that the intestinal capacity to finely process plant matter increases with age.
facts.quote: El aumento de la cantidad de gastrolitos en los adultos mayores puede ser indicativo de que la capacidad intestinal de procesar finamente la materia vegetal aumenta con la edad.

facts.statement: Isotope analysis shows that adult Limusaurus consistently matches the isotopic signatures of other herbivorous dinosaurs, while juveniles and subadults vary significantly in their signatures.
facts.quote: Un análisis de isótopos de los especímenes disponibles de Limusaurus también mostraron que los adultos coinciden consistentemente con las firmas isotópicas de otros dinosaurios herbívoros, sin embargo, en el mismo análisis, se encontró que los juveniles y los subadultos varían mucho en sus firmas isotópicas.

facts.statement: This indicates that juveniles were likely omnivores but shifted to strict herbivory as they aged.
facts.quote: Esto indica que los juveniles probablemente eran omnívoros, pero cambiaron a una estricta herbivoría a medida que envejecían.
